issue: Can the First Step Act's prospective-only change to § 924(c) stacking be an extraordinary and compelling reason for a compassionate release sentence reduction, including under U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)?

sides.position: The § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment cannot be an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction, because that would give the prospective-only amendment retroactive effect Congress withheld; U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) does not change this.
cases: United States v. Andrews, 12 F.4th 255 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Rutherford, 120 F.4th 360 (3d Cir. 2024)
United States v. Austin, 125 F.4th 688 (5th Cir. 2025)
United States v. McCall, 56 F.4th 1048 (6th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Crandall, 25 F.4th 582 (8th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Jenkins, 50 F.4th 1185 (D.C. Cir. 2022)
United States v. Black, No. 24-1191 (7th Cir. 2025)

sides.position: The § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment can be an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction, at least as channeled through U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6), which the Commission could validly adopt under 28 U.S.C. § 994(t).
cases: United States v. Ruvalcaba, 26 F.4th 14 (1st Cir. 2022)
United States v. McCoy, 981 F.3d 271 (4th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Chen, 48 F.4th 1092 (9th Cir. 2022)
United States v. McGee, 992 F.3d 1035 (10th Cir. 2021)

this_court: The majority follows Thacker and holds that the anti-stacking amendment cannot be an extraordinary and compelling reason, joining the Third Circuit. A separate writing argues for the opposing view that § 1B1.13(b)(6) is a reasonable exercise of the Commission's delegated authority and would remand.
quote: We recognize Thacker's holding that § 924(c)'s anti-stacking amendment cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction is not consensus; the courts of appeals have split on the issue.
cite: United States v. Eural Black, No. 24-1191 (7th Cir. 2025)
